facts.text: Director Sandor Stern started out as a medical doctor before turning to film, which is why a lifelike anatomy dummy in a doctor's office appealed to him.
Studio New World Pictures needed an American cast member for the film, which is how Terry O'Quinn (Dr. Frank Linden) landed the part.
The voice of Pin, the talking anatomy dummy, is Jonathan Banks, who is credited as the dummy's voice.
Dr. Linden speaking through Pin by ventriloquism isn't in Andrew Neiderman's novel. Director Sandor Stern added the ventriloquism for the film, according to The Bedlam Files.
Director Sandor Stern worked with novelist Andrew Neiderman for five years adapting Neiderman's 1981 novel before New World Pictures took it on.
Novelist Andrew Neiderman, who wrote the book Pin, later became the ghostwriter of the V.C. Andrews books, including the Flowers in the Attic series.
Pin the dummy is fully anatomically correct, a fact that drives some of the film's most disturbing scenes, like the sex-education lecture Dr. Frank Linden gives his children.
The dance-scene tunes, including On the Run, were written by Larry Weir and performed by a band called Pleasant Company.
Leon was David Hewlett's first leading role. He was 19 when he played the lonely, disturbed teen who believes an anatomy dummy is alive, according to Richard Scheib's Moria review.
Director Sandor Stern also wrote the screenplay for the original The Amityville Horror (1979), and later wrote and directed Amityville: The Evil Escapes.
Pin's voice is Jonathan Banks, later known as ex-cop fixer Mike Ehrmantraut on Breaking Bad. His dummy voice speaks right now, as Leon's sister Ursula is told it's no use asking Pin for help.
Cynthia Preston (Ursula) later spent three years as Faith Roscoe on the soap General Hospital, and she is credited here as Cyndy Preston in some listings.
David Hewlett, who plays Leon, later became Dr. Rodney McKay across three Stargate series, including a lead role in Stargate: Atlantis.
Leon's actor David Hewlett and Ursula's actress Cynthia Preston had already worked together on the Canadian horror anthology series The Darkside before playing siblings here.
Bad timing hurt the film: New World Pictures was dissolving its film division as Pin finished, so it dropped the planned theatrical release and sent the film straight to video in the US.
Pin gets a shout-out in the John Goodman movie Matinee (1989), and again in the cult horror film May (2002).
At a test screening, the projection started over an hour late and the audience mocked the film. New World's money troubles meant there was no second screening.
Producer Pierre David had a deal with Universal and pitched Pin to the studio first. Universal passed on it, and the film went to New World Pictures instead.
Terry O'Quinn played the title killer in The Stepfather (1987) a year before this, and later won an Emmy as John Locke on Lost.
The film never settles whether Pin is truly alive or only exists in Leon's head, according to Richard Scheib's Moria review. That ambiguity is a big part of its cult appeal.
Pin the dummy was a major expense: about $70,000 of the film's roughly $3 million (Canadian) budget went to building him.
Pin is the only theatrical feature directed by Sandor Stern. His other directing credits are TV movies, though he wrote the screenplay for the original The Amityville Horror.
John Pyper-Ferguson, who plays Stan Fraker, later played Peter Hutter on The Adventures of Brisco County, Jr. and Jack Soloff on Suits.
Pierre David had backed director Sandor Stern for years. When David visited the set to see the first week of footage, he was unhappy, and he had expected a more straightforward horror film.
The movie Leon sees on a date is David Cronenberg's Scanners (1981). David Hewlett later starred in the sequel Scanners II: The New Order (1991).
Executive producer Pierre David had produced several David Cronenberg films. Cronenberg was shooting Dead Ringers, another twisted-siblings story, around the same time as Pin.
Richard Scheib of Moria gave Pin three stars. He said he expected a story about a living ventriloquist's dummy and found 'a fascinating and surprisingly well-made Canadian horror film.'
The film leaves out most of the incest content from Andrew Neiderman's novel, and the Paperbacks from Hell write-up calls the movie relatively bloodless.
Janet Maslin of The New York Times called Pin 'a cool, bloodless, well-made thriller with a taste for the quietly bizarre.'
facts.byline: Janet Maslin — The New York Times

facts.text: The Movie Waffler called Pin a crossbreed of Psycho and Magic, the 1978 ventriloquist-dummy thriller, with the syrupy sheen of a made-for-TV Hallmark film.
Andrew Marshall of Starburst gave it 9 out of 10, calling it 'subtle, disturbing, and brilliant' at a time when horror was swamped with invincible serial killers.
Pin was shot in Quebec in 1987, with filming locations including Iberville and Saint-Lambert.
Pin had plenty of competition in 1988. One count puts the year's horror releases at 86, which helps explain how a quiet psychological chiller got lost.
Fangoria magazine included Pin in its '101 Best Horror Movies You've Never Seen,' helping it grow into a cult favorite.
The film's ending departs from the bleaker finish of Andrew Neiderman's novel, according to The Bedlam Files.
Pin got a second life in December 1991, when prints in Manhattan and San Francisco had successful runs and many critics said the film had been overlooked.
A Pin remake, to be directed again by Sandor Stern, was announced in 2011. Stern and novelist Andrew Neiderman reportedly disliked the pitch.
David Hewlett called Pin a 'creepy little movie that I starred in' and said 'There should be a sequel.' Director Sandor Stern called it the best filmmaking experience of his career.
